newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen softer at open, awaits GDP data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen softer at open, awaits GDP data.

text.p: Wall Street shares are expected to open slightly softer Thursday, taking early cues from a stream of economic data but vulnerable to profit-taking after the recent run-up.
Stocks, which soared to new highs on Wednesday as bond yields slid, today face data on second quarter gross domestic product, weekly jobless claims and the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index for July.
Bonds and stocks are also looking anxiously toward Friday's release of July jobs data, analysts said.

"We have a slew of economic numbers coming out," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "Markets are so enriched with optimism that any slight number which is not viewed positively could send the bond market down and prompt profit-taking in the Dow."
GDP data, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are expected to show an annual growth rate of 1.9 percent in the second quarter, compared to 5.9 percent in the first quarter.

If the GDP figures appear benign, as expected, bonds and stocks could rise, analysts said. "If these numbers show a decent slowdown -- and there is no reason to think they won't -- markets could do better," said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.
Jobless claims for the week ended July 26 are also due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. They are forecast to rise to 306,000 from 299,000 in the previous week.
Chicago PMI is due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast a July reading of 59.8, down from 61.5 in June.
Ahead of the data, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index lost 2.35 points to 954.80.
The long bond, which fell to its lowest yield this year on Wednesday, was down 4/32 to 6.34 percent.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied yesterday as interest rates fell, taking an optimistic stance on economic growth and inflation. It finished 80 points higher at 8255.
The dollar slipped against the yen in Tokyo as the market became cautious about U.S.-Japanese trade relations. It was trading at 117.75/80 yen.
In Europe the dollar was trading at 1.8316/26 marks.
Japan's Nikkei average closed up 118.61 points, or 0.59 percent, at 20,331.43.
In London the FTSE 100 was up 2.6 points at 4929.9.
U.S. stocks were little changed in London trading.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that some investors believe AMC Entertainment Inc might be a bargain, as the chief exective's health problems stir speculation about a company takeover.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that Congress and White House budget negotiators backed away from a plan that would have raised capital gains taxes on some sales.
